CHAPTER LXXI

“As is the race of leaves so is that of men.” And a great man budded
unnoticed in a tailor's house at Rotterdam this year, and a large man
dropped to earth with great eclat.

Philip, Duke of Burgundy, Earl of Holland, etc., etc., lay sick at
Bruges. Now paupers got sick and got well as Nature pleased; but woe
betided the rich in an age when, for one Mr. Malady killed three fell by
Dr. Remedy.

The Duke's complaint, nameless then, is now diphtheria. It is, and was,
a very weakening malady, and the Duke was old; so altogether Dr. Remedy
bled him.

The Duke turned very cold: wonderful!

Then Dr. Remedy had recourse to the arcana of science.

“Ho! This is grave. Flay me an ape incontinent, and clap him to the
Duke's breast!”

Officers of state ran septemvious, seeking an ape, to counteract the
bloodthirsty tomfoolery of the human species.

Perdition! The duke was out of apes. There were buffaloes, lizards,
Turks, leopards; any unreasonable beast but the right one.

“Why, there used to be an ape about,” said one. “If I stand here I saw
him.”

So there used; but the mastiff had mangled the sprightly creature for
stealing his supper; and so fulfilled the human precept, “Soyez de votre
siecle!”

In this emergency the seneschal cast his despairing eyes around; and not
in vain. A hopeful light shot into them.

“Here is this,” said he, sotto voce. “Surely this will serve: 'tis
altogether apelike, doublet and hose apart.”

“Nay,” said the chancellor peevishly, “the Princess Marie would hang us.
She doteth on this.”

Now this was our friend Giles, strutting, all unconscious, in cloth of
gold.

Then Dr. Remedy grew impatient, and bade flay a dog.

“A dog is next best to an ape; only it must be a dog all of one colour.”

So they flayed a liver-coloured dog, and clapped it, yet palpitating, to
their sovereign's breast and he died.

Philip the Good, thus scientifically disposed of, left thirty-one
children: of whom one, somehow or another, was legitimate; and reigned
in his stead.

The good duke provided for nineteen out of the other thirty; the rest
shifted for themselves.

According to the Flemish chronicle the deceased prince was descended
from the kings of Troy through Thierry of Aquitaine, and Chilperic,
Pharamond, etc., the old kings of Franconia.

But this in reality was no distinction. Not a prince of his day have
I been able to discover who did not come down from Troy. “Priam” was
mediaeval for “Adam.”

The good duke's, body was carried into Burgundy, and laid in a noble
mausoleum of black marble at Dijon.

Holland rang with his death; and little dreamed that anything as
famous was born in her territory that year. That judgment has been long
reversed. Men gaze at the tailor's house, here the great birth of the
fifteenth century took place. In what house the good duke died “no one
knows and no one cares,” as the song says.

And why?

Dukes Philip the Good come and go, and leave mankind not a halfpenny
wiser, nor better, nor other than they found it.

But when, once in three hundred years, such a child is born to the world
as Margaret's son, lo! a human torch lighted by fire from heaven; and
“FIAT LUX” thunder's from pole to pole.

[Reference Original]: CHAPTER TWO.
[Reference Rewrite]: To comprehend the architecture of my early exile, one must first understand the absolute poverty of my universe at the age of seven. I existed within a microscopic empire of two, subjugated by a man I was conditioned to call "Master." He was a square-built, brutal artifact of a world I did not know, roughly sixty years of age, though time on the island seemed measured only by the decay of his humanity. His dark hair fell in matted, feral clusters, and a vast beard obscured his face, rendering him less a man than a beast draped in the ruin of whatever civilization had cast him out. He possessed a terrifying latent power, yet he spent his days in a state of stagnant lethargy, only stirring to exert his dominance over my labor—collecting sea-birds or hauling faggots of wood down the ravine.

Our lives were bound by the daily ritual of bathing in a salt-water pool, barricaded from the shark-infested ocean by a ridge of jagged stone. Beyond this, my existence was an enforced void. I was permitted no education, no heritage, and almost no language. The Master utilized silence as a tool of oppression, rationing his words to commands and curses, ensuring my mind remained as barren as the rocky crags that caged us. I became a taciturn creature, my intellect starved, left to gaze into the abyssal depths of the ocean or trace the cold geometries of the stars. I was kept as a beast of the field—valuable only for the calories my labor saved him, and perhaps to serve as a mirror for his own desperate need for mastery.

[Reference Original]: CHAPTER THREE.

I left him, and commenced a careful descent of the precipices by which we were surrounded, but, before I had gone fifty paces, another flash of lightning was followed up by a loud shriek, which arrested my steps. Where the noise came from I could not tell, but I heard my companion calling to me to come back. I obeyed him, and found him standing where I had left him.

"You called me, master?"

"Yes, I did; take my hand and lead me to the cabin."

I obeyed him, wondering why he asked me so to do. He gained his bed-place, and threw himself down on it.

"Bring the kid full of water," said he--"quick!"

I brought it, and he bathed his head and face. After a time, he threw himself back upon the bed-place, and groaned heavily.

"O God! It's all over with me," said he at last. "I shall live and die in this cursed hole."

"What's the matter, master?" said I.
[Reference Rewrite]: I left him in the dark, initiating a careful descent down the rain-slicked precipices that formed the carceral walls of our world. Before I had traversed fifty paces, a sudden rupture of lightning tore the sky, pursued instantly by a shriek so guttural it arrested my breath. It was a sound stripped of all former sovereignty. I could not trace its origin through the howling wind, but then I heard the voice—his voice, diminished and frantic—commanding my return.

I obeyed, stepping back over the jagged stone, and found him frozen exactly where I had left him.

"You called me, master?" I asked, testing the word on my tongue.

"Yes, I did. Take my hand. Lead me to the cabin."

I guided him, marveling at the sudden frailty in his grip. The hand that had so often struck me down now clung to my shoulder with the desperate dependency of a drowning man. He found his bedding and collapsed onto it, a ruined monument of flesh.

"Bring the kid full of water," he gasped. "Quick!"

I brought the vessel. He plunged his face into it, bathing his head as if trying to wash away the fire of the heavens. Presently, he fell back against the damp wood, a heavy groan escaping his chest. "O God! It is all over with me," he whispered into the gloom. "I shall live and die in this cursed hole."

"What is the matter, master?" I asked.

He offered no answer, sinking instead into a rhythmic liturgy of curses and moans. When he finally fell still, I slipped out again into the dying tempest.

In the quiet, unassuming shadow of a tailor's workshop in Rotterdam, a great soul budded unnoticed this year, while simultaneously, a colossal figure crashed to earth with deafening fanfare. At Bruges, Philip, Duke of Burgundy, Earl of Holland, and myriad other titles, lay wasting away in fever. Here, nature allowed the poor to fall ill and recover with equal indifference; but woe betide the wealthy in an era where a single Mr. Malady could decimate three, while Dr. Remedy struggled to save one. The Duke's affliction, unnamed in those days, is now known as diphtheria—a cruel, weakening scourge that claimed the old man. Consequently, Dr. Remedy resorted to the ancient, bloody art of leeching. The Duke turned icy cold, a testament to the failure of mercy. Desperate, the physician turned to the arcane sciences of his time. "Ho! This is grave," he cried, demanding, "Flay an ape incontinent and clamp it to the Duke's breast!" State officers scrambled in every direction, seeking a primate to counteract the bloodthirsty folly of their own kind. Perdition! No apes remained. Buffaloes, lizards, Turks, and leopards roamed free, but none were the requisite beast. "Why, there used to be an ape about," one officer muttered. "If I stood here, I saw him." Indeed, there had been; but a mastiff, driven by hunger, had mauled the sprightly creature for stealing its supper, fulfilling the grim human precept: *Be of your season*. In this emergency, the seneschal cast his despairing eyes around the room, and hope flickered. "Here is this," he whispered, holding up a specimen. "Surely this will serve: 'tis altogether apelike, doublet and hose apart." "Nay," snapped the Chancellor peevishly, "the Princess Marie would hang us. She dotes on this." Thus spoke our friend Giles, strutting unconsciously in cloth of gold, oblivious to the gravity of the moment. Dr. Remedy, growing impatient with the bureaucracy of life and death, commanded, "Flay a dog." "A dog is next best to an ape," he reasoned, adding the condition, "only it must be a dog of one color." They skinned a liver-colored hound and pinned its still-palpating heart to the sovereign's chest. The Duke died. Philip the Good, thus scientifically disposed of, left behind thirty-one children; of these, one, by some miracle of lineage, was legitimate and ascended to rule. The benevolent duke had provided for nineteen of the others; the remainder were forced to shift for themselves. According to the Flemish chronicles, the deceased prince descended from the kings of Troy through Thierry of Aquitaine, Chilperic, Pharamond, and the ancient monarchs of Franconia. Yet, this genealogy held no true distinction. Not a single prince of his day can be discovered who does not claim descent from Troy. "Priam" was merely medieval code for "Adam." The Duke's body was carried into Burgundy and interred in a noble mausoleum of black marble at Dijon. Holland rang with mourning for his passing, little dreaming that within its borders, something as famous as a new sun was being born that same year. That judgment has since been utterly reversed. All eyes now turn to the tailor's house, the site of the great birth of the fifteenth century. As for the house where the good duke breathed his last, "no one knows and no one cares," as the song goes. Why? For Dukes like Philip the Good come and go, leaving mankind neither a halfpenny wiser, nor better, nor different than they found it. But when, once in three hundred years, such a child is born to the world as Margaret's son, behold! A human torch ignited by fire from heaven; and "FIAT LUX"—Let there be Light—thunders from pole to pole.
